artworks.title: Tantalus
artworks.description: Assereto's Genoese canvas shows the Pelopid king reaching for fruit and water that forever recede — the underworld feast that made his name a verb for torment just out of reach.

artworks.title: Tantalus
artworks.artist: Hendrick Goltzius, after Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem
artworks.description: From The Four Disgracers: Goltzius engraves Tantalus hurtling through empty air — the king who served his son to the gods, falling toward the hunger and thirst that await him below.

artworks.title: Tantalus
artworks.description: A Venetian tenebrist treatment of the standing sinner: Tantalus half-submerged, straining toward what he cannot grasp — the classic Tartarean punishment of the feast denied.

artworks.title: Tantalus
artworks.description: A Prado canvas in Ribera's manner keeps the lost Furia alive: the underworld king twisted in shadow, still reaching for the water and fruit that slip away — Tantalus as Spanish Baroque torment.

popCulture.title: Tantalize
popCulture.description: English tantalize means to torment with what stays just out of reach — the Pelopid king's underworld feast turned into an everyday verb.

popCulture.title: Tantalum
popCulture.description: The element tantalum was named for Tantalus — a metal that, like his water and fruit, resists being taken, hard to extract from its ore.

popCulture.title: House of Atreus
popCulture.description: The Atreid curse begins with Tantalus' crime against the gods — the Pelopid feast that seeds Agamemnon's house and the Oresteia's inherited blood-guilt.
